papers.title: Re(Visiting) Time Series Foundation Models in Finance
papers.abstract: Financial time series forecasting is vital for trading, portfolio optimization, and risk management but is challenged by noisy, nonstationary, and heterogeneous data. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), inspired by large language models, aim to learn transferable temporal representations. Whether pre-training on massive, diverse datasets enables similar generalization to finance remains an open question. This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of TSFMs in global financial markets using large-scale daily excess-return data. We assess zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, and pre-training from scratch against strong benchmarks. Off-the-shelf TSFMs generally perform poorly, while finance-native pre-training improves long-window gross portfolio performance. Larger pre-training datasets and synthetic augmentation improve selected specifications, particularly at longer input windows. Configuration changes have mixed effects across forecasting and portfolio metrics, and TSFMs do not consistently outperform strong benchmarks. These findings caution against uncritical AI adoption in finance, where insufficient validation can lead to unreliable forecasts and substantial financial losses.

papers.title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
papers.abstract: Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

papers.title: Mean--Variance Portfolio Selection by Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning: Algorithms, Regret Analysis, and Empirical Study
papers.abstract: We study continuous-time mean--variance portfolio selection in markets where stock prices are diffusion processes driven by observable factors that are also diffusion processes, yet the coefficients of these processes are unknown. Based on the recently developed reinforcement learning (RL) theory for diffusion processes, we present a general data-driven RL approach that learns the pre-committed investment strategy directly without attempting to learn or estimate the market coefficients. For multi-stock Black--Scholes markets without factors, we further devise an algorithm and prove its performance guarantee by deriving a sublinear regret bound in terms of the Sharpe ratio. We then carry out an extensive empirical study implementing this algorithm to compare its performance and trading characteristics, evaluated under a host of common metrics, with a large number of widely employed portfolio allocation strategies on S\&P 500 constituents. The results demonstrate that the proposed continuous-time RL strategy is consistently among the best, especially in a volatile bear market, and decisively outperforms the model-based continuous-time counterparts by significant margins.

papers.title: A Second Order Transport Scheme for Dynamic Portfolio Subspaces under a Varying Risk Metric
papers.abstract: We analyze the transport of portfolio exposures between moving subspaces under a varying positive definite risk metric. The reference evolution is the induced connection obtained from the ambient connection of minimum norm in fixed asset coordinates. An explicit expansion of risk weighted Procrustes identifies a leading local error that couples metric deformation with covariant motion normal to the subspace. A rank two construction with an exact continuous solution shows that this term can reduce global accuracy to first order even when the metric commutes with its derivative. Geometric mean alignment and a symmetric Procrustes construction cancel the term and yield reversible updates with second order global accuracy. We establish uniform error bounds on nonuniform partitions, characterize the cases in which the Procrustes defect vanishes, and distinguish discretization error from errors in estimated geometry. We also characterize the connection induced by principal square root whitening and its relation to the selected transport. Manufactured examples confirm the predicted defect and convergence rates. A historical geometry stress test then estimates the defect from preceding observations and finds that it predicts the subsequent separation between risk weighted Procrustes and both second order updates, while the two second order schemes remain much closer to each other. Portfolio comparisons separately evaluate target persistence, turnover, and economic implementation.

papers.title: Principal component error in high-dimensional factor models
papers.abstract: In a statistical factor model, principal components (or eigenvectors) of a sample covariance matrix serve as estimates of principal directions, the true drivers of co-movement of a collection of observed variables. We write the often substantial error in these estimates as a sum of two interpretable terms, which we show have almost sure asymptotic limits as the number of variables grows with sample size bounded. This scenario is commonplace in financial economics, genomics, machine learning and signal processing. Out-of-subspace error measures the distance from an estimate to the subspace spanned by population factor exposures. It can be expressed in terms of data, providing an estimable floor for asymptotic error. In-subspace error is driven by a rotation error within that subspace, which arises from the fixed sample size of the latent factor returns and cannot be estimated from data alone. We illustrate our error analysis with a three-factor simulation of the US public equity market, showing the dependence of the magnitude of the error and its components on dimension and sample size. In that simulation, out-of-subspace error dominates. Researchers who rely on principal component analysis to estimate factor models can use our results to quantify errors in model-based predictions and attributions.

papers.title: Dynamic portfolio selection under generalized disappointment aversion
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the continuous-time portfolio selection problem under generalized disappointment aversion (GDA). The implicit definition of the certainty equivalent within GDA preferences introduces time inconsistency to this problem. Within the class of bounded, right-continuous deterministic strategies, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for equilibrium in the form of a fully nonlinear integral equation. Investigating the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the integral equation, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the equilibrium in this class. Our findings indicate that under disappointment aversion preferences, non-participation in the stock market is the unique equilibrium in this class. The semi-analytical equilibrium strategies obtained under the constant relative risk aversion utility functions reveal that, under GDA preferences, the investment proportion in the stock market consistently remains smaller than the investment proportion under classical expected utility theory. The numerical analysis shows that the equilibrium strategy's monotonicity concerning the two parameters of GDA preference aligns with the monotonicity of the degree of risk aversion. Finally, in a switching-drift market with a random expected return, we prove the existence of a non-deterministic equilibrium.

papers.title: On the Structure of Risk Contribution: A Leave-One-Out Decomposition into Inherent and Correlation Risk
papers.abstract: Risk Contribution (RC) is a widely used risk attribution metric that assigns each position a share of portfolio volatility, with contributions that sum to total portfolio volatility. This paper proposes a leave-one-out decomposition of RC into two interpretable components at the position level: an inherent term (position's own scaled variance) and a correlation term (covariance with the other holdings). Unlike the X-sigma-rho framework, which uses the position's correlation with the full portfolio, ICD uses covariance with the other holdings, yielding qualitatively different diagnostic signals when a position is large relative to the portfolio. The contribution is the interpretive framing and an exact identity linking the components to incremental volatility (iVol), which allows the discrete condition under which a position reduces portfolio volatility to be stated in closed form. That condition differs from the marginal condition and the two can disagree for over-hedged or levered positions. The decomposition also inherits RC's strict additivity. Empirical illustrations on three multi-asset portfolios show the components shift differently across regimes, distinguishing stand-alone volatility spikes from correlation breakdown, and demonstrate value for risk reporting, stress testing, and attribution.

papers.title: Harvesting the Variance Risk Premium in Nuclear and Energy Equities: A Short-Put Portfolio Derisking Strategy
papers.abstract: We study whether nuclear and energy-adjacent equity options carry a harvestable variance risk premium. Using CRSP and OptionMetrics data for 2000-2024 on a universe of 49 optioned securities under 41 ticker labels, at-the-money implied volatility exceeds the volatility realized over the following 21 trading days in 18 of 25 years, and 29 of 41 tickers show a positive premium on signal days with t-statistics above 2. A fully mechanical cash-secured short-put book sells one put per name per month near 0.25 delta and 45 days to expiry, and exits on the first touch of take-profit at half premium, stop-loss at twice premium, or a 0.50-delta stop, marked daily at validated quote midpoints. Equal-weight and inverse-volatility weightings earn 8.3% and 7.1% a year at Sharpe ratios of 0.98 and 0.99 with maximum drawdowns of 16% and 13%, versus 15.5% a year, a Sharpe ratio of 0.80, and a 46% drawdown for an equal-weight stock book; in 2008 the put book loses 9.5% against the stock book's 37.2%, and the monthly correlation between the two is 0.62. Performance is reported before transaction costs, on a fixed present-day universe.
